title: Peter's first sermon (Acts 2:14–41)
hook: the man who denied him now preaches, and three thousand are baptized
tomorrow: Silver and gold I have none

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthias, chosen for the empty place. Your line was they prayed first.

Not long ago, a servant girl in a courtyard asked Peter a simple question, aren't you one of his? And he said he wasn't. Now it's the feast of Pentecost, and Jerusalem is full of devout pilgrims, Luke says, from every nation under heaven. The disciples have just poured out of a house, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking in languages they never learned, and a crowd has gathered to stare. Some people laugh: they're drunk. And the man who stands up to answer them is Peter.
screen: `A SERVANT GIRL'S QUESTION.` → `PENTECOST, THE CITY PACKED.` → `PETER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: His opening line is almost a joke. These men aren't drunk, as you suppose; it's only the third hour of the day, nine in the morning. Then he gets serious. He quotes the prophet Joel: in the last days, God says, I will pour out my spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, young men shall see visions, old men shall dream dreams. This, Peter says, is that. He tells them about Jesus of Nazareth, his miracles, his death, and that God raised him up, and we are all witnesses. There's that word witness again. He quotes the psalms of David, and ends on the claim that God has made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. Luke says the listeners were cut to the heart. They ask, what shall we do? And Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins: and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." Do penance follows the Latin. The Greek word, metanoēsate, means change your mind, turn around, a whole new direction. That day, Luke says, about three thousand were added. And consider who's speaking. Not a polished speaker. A fisherman who, only weeks earlier, couldn't stand up to a servant girl. That courage didn't come from practice. Acts is clear about where it came from: the Spirit poured out that morning. The coward preached. And Catholics often call that feast the Church's birthday.
screen: `NOT DRUNK: IT'S NINE A.M.` · `JOEL: THIS IS THAT.` · `CUT TO THE HEART.` · `THREE THOUSAND, THAT DAY.` · then, large: `PETER'S FIRST SERMON.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment coming up where you usually stay quiet: a meeting, a family dinner, a friend saying something unkind, a chance to say what you believe. Picture opening your mouth there and saying one true sentence, plainly and kindly, and feel your feet on the floor while you imagine it. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for the courage Peter was given; if you don't, simply rehearse the sentence.
Pentecost. The feast when Peter, the fisherman who once denied Jesus, stood up before the crowd, and about three thousand were baptized. Today's word.
Your line: the coward preached. Weeks after the courtyard, the crowd. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Pentecost at the close of the Easter season, reading Acts 2 at Mass, and the Church often calls the day its birthday; adults are often received into the Church at Easter after a period of preparation.

what it means: a man who failed badly, now speaking with a courage Acts credits to the Spirit.
what a scholar hears: Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32 and Psalm 16 (Douay 15) and Psalm 110 (109); the Vulgate's paenitentiam agite gives the Douay's do penance for metanoēsate.

chat.says: How did Peter go from denying Jesus to preaching to thousands?
options: Acts says it came from the Spirit poured out at Pentecost, not from practice.
He'd spent years training as a public speaker before he met Jesus.
The crowd was small and friendly, so it didn't take much courage.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: Acts 2:38's Greek is metanoēsate, not metanoeite (teach, match, myth). Also removed uncited counts ('seven weeks', 'fifty days after Passover', 'in front of thousands'); the denial now follows the cited John 18:17; 'the third hour' now from Acts 2:15; 'the Church dates its beginning' softened; howItsDone drops 'fifty days after Easter'.

Peter's speech in Acts 2:22–36 addresses the crowd's share in the crucifixion; the teach deliberately does not frame it as blame on the Jewish people (see Nostra Aetate 4). Keeper to confirm the summary is fair to the text.
Acts 2:38 Douay wording: verify exactly ('Do penance, and be baptized every one of you…').
Pentecost as the Church's birthday: common Catholic expression (cf. CCC 1076). Confirm.
'Seven weeks' from the denial to Pentecost: roughly fifty days. Confirm.
